# Cup Day, a dead coolroom and 14 bags of servo ice

Dear Jonno,

Since you’ve asked me about the coolroom approximately 400 times since you saw my story, here you go. A whole blog post for you and the other 39 people who read this thing. Hi Mum.

First of all, London has made you soft. I know you’re going to message me saying you’ve worked worse services, but you weren’t here and I was, so unfortunately I get to tell the story however I want. You would’ve cried.

The coolroom compressor died sometime overnight between Monday and Tuesday. I found it at 6.40 on Cup Day morning. Opened the door, looked at the thermometer and saw 11 degrees.

Eleven.

Not ideal for a room whose entire job is being cold.

I stood there for a second doing that thing where you look at a thermometer again in case it’s having a laugh. It wasn’t. We had 140 covers booked for lunch, a three-course set menu, and the coolroom had decided it was time for a holiday.

Raff was away that day, so I was running it. Which meant I got the special treat of making all the phone calls and trying to work out what could be saved.

Wally from Coldline couldn’t come until Wednesday, and the part had to come from Sydney. So there was no quick fix. We were doing Cup Day without a coolroom.

Phil’s contribution was “just make it work, mate.”

Thanks, Phil. I’ll let the compressor know.

We started shifting everything we could into the two undercounters and the bar fridge. Marta next door let us use half her walk-in, which saved our arses. Even so, we lost about $1,800 worth of stock, mostly dairy and the duck legs. That part was shit, obviously, but there wasn’t much time to stand around mourning a bucket of cream.

Then came the beef.

Me and Benny had 30 kilos of beef shin to get down the laneway to Marta’s. We put it on a milk crate trolley, because apparently that was the best transport solution available to two grown men in a professional kitchen. It was raining, naturally, and one of the wheels fell off.

So there we were in the laneway on Cup Day, wrestling a busted trolley full of beef shin in the rain. Benny was trying to keep it upright, I was trying not to drop the beef, and the trolley was doing its best to lie down.

You would have had a lot to say about the trolley, right up until you were asked to help. Then suddenly you’d have an urgent garnish situation inside.

A lady on table 9 saw us out the window. Later she asked if the beef was “free range from the laneway”. Fair question. She’d seen more of its journey than most customers ever do.

Meanwhile, Kev took the old esky to the servo for ice. Fourteen bags. The bloke behind the counter asked if he was having a party.

Technically, yes. A party for 140 people, none of whom knew they were attending the world’s least relaxing picnic.

Kev kept us going with that esky. Dishy, ice runner, emergency logistics manager. Give the man a title and a pay rise. Phil, if you’re one of the 40 readers, I’m serious about that bit.

We managed to get set up, more or less. There were things in fridges they’d never been in before, things next door at Marta’s, and a lot of us trying to remember which was which. Every time someone needed something, it felt like a small expedition. But everyone just got on with it.

At 12.15 we had to 86 the panna cotta. Just a lovely calm time to change a dessert on a three-course set menu.

Dessert became “affogato with whatever”, which is about as accurate a description as I can give you now. And people loved it. More than the panna cotta, possibly. You spend all that time planning a menu and apparently what the people really want is for your coolroom to die so you start chucking things near coffee.

I’m still annoyed about that.

The mad thing is, once service got going, it was honestly the best one we’ve done all year. Everyone was locked in. Benny was on it, Kev was everywhere, and nobody had time to carry on. We just fed them.

You know those services where everyone’s in the right spot and calls are actually getting heard? Like that, except with half our food living next door and an esky doing the work of a major appliance.

I reckon you would’ve loved it, actually. After the initial crying. You’d have spent the whole service yelling about the bar fridge, then brought it up every Friday for the next five years.

Marta reckons we owe her for the walk-in space in croissant credit. Fair enough. At this rate I owe her about three weeks of staff meal. Still cheaper than trying to fit 30 kilos of beef shin into Phil’s car with the air con on.

Oh, and my horse in the sweep was called **Ice Cold Lad**. Came second last.

So even the horse was taking the piss.

Anyway, that’s what happened. We lost a heap of stock, the panna cotta got the arse, Benny nearly lost a wheel in the laneway and Kev bought enough ice to concern a servo attendant. Then we somehow had our best service of the year.

Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite.

Hope London’s treating you well, mate. Come home, ya flog.
